claims.text: Controlled thermal and mechanical processing can produce a finely dispersed nanoscale dual-phase microstructure with aluminum enrichment at grain boundaries in a lightweight HEA.
This engineered microstructure enables low density to be combined with high mechanical strength.
This engineered microstructure improves corrosion resistance.
This engineered microstructure improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Vacuum-arc melting can be used to produce lightweight HEAs.
The proposed initial alloy has a homogeneous solid-solution state with minimal uncontrolled elemental segregation.
Keeping copper content low helps avoid localized corrosion associated with copper segregation.
A heat-treatment-plus-deformation or additive-manufacturing intervention can induce and stabilize the proposed nanoscale architecture.
Testing across strain rates can distinguish grain-boundary slip from dislocation slip behavior.
Oxidation testing around 200°C is an appropriate test of the proposed high-temperature oxidation mechanism.
Nanoscale heterogeneity and fine grains facilitate grain-boundary strengthening.
Aluminum enrichment at nanoscale grain boundaries promotes in-situ formation of a protective oxide film during corrosive exposure.
Aluminum enrichment at nanoscale grain boundaries promotes in-situ formation of a protective oxide film during elevated-temperature exposure.
The processed alloy will have higher yield strength than a same-composition conventionally processed control.
The processed alloy will have lower corrosion current density than the control in 0.6 M NaCl.
The processed alloy will undergo less oxidation degradation than the control around 200°C.
Excessive copper segregation decreases corrosion performance by accelerating localized corrosion.
The proposed synergistic benefits cease if the processing fails to produce the desired dual-phase microstructure.
Excessive phase segregation, particularly copper segregation, can negate corrosion benefits even when passivating elements are present.
The optimal balance between useful phase dispersion and harmful elemental segregation is not established.
